column6: Callisto | Moon of Jupiter | Solar System
column7: Callisto is believed to have the most heavily cratered surface in the Solar System. It is also believed to be the oldest undisturbed surface in the Solar System, as Callisto does not have a thick atmosphere or geologic activity. The moon may have a salty ocean under its surface, but life would have to adapt to extreme cold. However, one hypothesis suggests that comets and asteroids delivered the necessary ingredients for life to planets through impacts in their early formation. Studying Callisto's surface could give us a snapshot of what molecules were present in the very early Solar System, billions of years ago.

column7: Ceres could be up to 30% water by mass. When clear images of Ceres were first published with bright spots visible in the craters, some thought they were alien cities. It&apos:s just very reflective salt: possible proof of an ocean underneath. When smaller asteroids strike Ceres, it cracks the surface and allows water to seep through. The liquid evaporates into space, leaving salt deposits behind.

column6: Enceladus | Moon of Saturn | Solar System
column7: More than a hundred geysers have been discovered on Enceladus, which shoot water, ice, minerals, and other molecules up to hundreds of miles above the surface. Some of it falls back to the surface as thick snow, while some floats away to form Saturn's fuzzy E Ring. The plumes are similar in composition to comets, which astronomers believe may have brought ice and organic molecules into the inner Solar System.

column6: Europa | Moon of Jupiter | Solar System
column7: Europa is strongly believed to have a megaocean underneath a thick crust of ice, which may be warmed by deep volcanic vents. On Earth, deep hydrothermal vents cycle minerals from the Earth&apos:s crust into the ocean and support biomes of extremophiles. If these conditions existed on Europa, they would be protected from harmful radiation by Europa&apos:s thick ice sheets. Europa is one of the strongest candidates in the Solar System for life. NASA&apos:s Europa Clipper mission, launched in 2024, will reach the moon in 2030, and aims to complete about 50 close flybys to gather more research. As part of their "Message in a Bottle" campaign, a fingernail-sized chip with the names of 2.6 million Earth residents will accompany Europa Clipper on its 1.8 billion mile journey.

column6: Ganymede | Moon of Jupiter | Solar System
column7: Ganymede is big enough to be a planet itself, but is caught it Jupiter's orbit. It is doubly protected by Jupiter's magnetic field and its own, likely generated by convection in its core. Evidence points to a massive ocean beneath a thick ice sheet surface. If Ganymede does have a hot core, the depths of this giant ocean may be warmed by undersea volcanic vents &emdash; similar to biomes found on Earth where extremophiles thrive.

column6: HD 216520c | Near Cassiopeia and Andromeda Constellations
column7: HD 216520c is a Neptune-like planet that orbits slightly closer than its star's Habitable Zone. Estimates of its radius could be as large as 3x the Earth. Temperature estimates also vary, with several hypotheses for possible atmospheres. Even so, HD 216520 c is still believed to be habitable.  Initially, planets of this size were believed to be mostly gas with no solid surface. New evidence suggests that mini-Neptunes are actually Super-Earth planets with thick, puffy atmospheres. HD 216520c may be revisited for more study in the future.

column6: Io | Moon of Jupiter | Solar System
column7: Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System. Jupiter's closest moon, it is constantly squeezed by strong tidal forces that cause magma to ooze into lakes of lava. These lakes are large enough to glow when viewed from Io' night side. Io may be far too hot and volatile for our understanding of life, but researching its volcanic properties teaches astronomers more about the geophysical forces that shape planets. Volcanism is important for shaping an early planet, cycling metals and minerals from the core that enrich the crust.

column7: Kepler-69c was once believed to be possible habitable, but is now hypothesized to be a "Super Venus". It wobbles in and out of its star's habitable zone, which combined with a thicker atmosphere may contribute to a runaway greenhouse effect. In the search for Earth-like life, studying analogs to inhospitable planets of our Solar System helps piece together the mystery of where planets diverge from potentially habitable to completely hostile.

column7: Kepler-62e, along with its neighbor 62f, are exciting candidates for habitable worlds. With 62e's estimated size of 1.6x the Earth, it is more likely to be a mini-Neptune than a super-Earth. Research shows that mini-Neptunes may actually be primordial super-Earths, and comparing 62e with the smaller 62f could show two similar planets that underwent slightly different formation processes. Kepler-62e may have Earth-like thermperatures &emdash; or its thick atmosphere could be trapping heat.

column7: Kepler-62f is a promising candidate for further study. It orbits at a similar distance to Venus, but recieves only as much sunlight as Mars. It is currently thought to be about 1.4x the radius of the Earth, but its mass could vary. If it is a denser planet, this may indicate the presence of a large water ocean.

column7: Mars was once much more volcanically active. It was possibly similar to Earth, with a water ocean covering much of the surface. However, its small size led to its core cooling, eventually weakening its magnetic field. Without a field to block radiation from the Sun, the atmosphere was stripped away, and water evaporated into space. Our cold desert neighbor was left behind.

column7:
A common misconception is that Mercury is extremely hot, since it is the closest planet to the Sun. Mercury is extremely hot — but only on one side. The planet spins so slowly that one side recieves scorching sunlight and radiation for an entire Mercury year, or 88 Earth days, while the other side is dark and freezing. Despite these extremes, water ice may exist at the poles, in craters so deep sunlight never reaches.
Mercury's composition of 70% iron is unique, and some astronomers believe it is rare in the universe. A large collision or other catastrophic event could have impacted its formation. Studying Mercury may provide more clues into the question of if our Solar System (and the life in it) are especially unique.

column7: Pluto is far too cold and small for Earth-like life, but showed that dwarf planets are more complex than we thought. Pluto's crust contains Nitrogen and water ice along with complex organic solids. It swaps some of its loose sediment with its moon and binary companion Charon through their shared, thin Nitrogen atmosphere. Many important molecules for life are hypothesized to come from comets, and Pluto shares the Kuiper Belt region with trillions. Pluto's flagship flyby mission, New Horizons, has continued into the Kuper Belt to attempt additional flybys of faraway objects.

column6: Titan | Moon of Saturn | Solar System
column7: Titan's atmosphere supports a weather cycle and seasons &emdash; but with methane, not water. ThTitan has fascinated astrobiologists for years, as it is covered in complex organic molecules while retaining a freezing, poisonous atmosphere. Measurements of Titan' gravity suggests that it may have a subsurface ocean, as many large moons of Jupiter and Saturn are suspected to. If this ocean exists, there are a very specific set of circumstances under which it could potentially support life. Titan would need an internal source of energy. Regardless if it proves to be habitable, Titan is notable as the only other example of an ongoing solid-liquid-gas cycle including precipitation.

column7: The first exoplanet found within its star's Habitable Zone, orbiting on the very inner edge. It is slightly larger than Earth but much, much denser, indicating it is likely rocky and metal-rich. It rotates very slowly, or may be locked with one side always facing the star. Astronomers are optimistic it has an atmosphere, because the TOI-700 system contains other planets closer to the star with thick atmospheres. If solar winds were not powerful enough to blow these atmospheres away from closer planets, TOI-700d having an atmosphere (possibly one able to circulate heat!) is promising.

column7: The discovery of the TRAPPIST-1 system by the Transiting Planets and Planetesimals Small Telescope in Chile began a new era in exoplanet exploration. TRAPPIST-1 d is very small, less than 40% of the Earth's mass. Its star is extremely cool, so TRAPPIST-1 likely has Earth-like temperatures despite orbiting very closely. The atmosphere of TRAPPIST-1d is still being studied. Very thick, cloudy atmospheres have been ruled out; this means it likely, but not certainly, has a very thin atmosphere. Astronomers also worry its small size means it does not have a strong magnetic field.

column7: Venus and Earth likely formed in a similar way. Venus may have supported liquid water at one point, but its thick atmosphere contains large amounts of gases that trap heat, such as CO2. Eventually Venus became so warm it is almost impossible to cool naturally. Studying Venus has given astronomers, meteorologists, and climate scientists a clearer understanding of how the atmosphere affects temperature, and helped us tackle excessive warming in our own atmosphere.

column7: The discovery of the TRAPPIST-1 system by the Transiting Planets and Planetesimals Small Telescope in Chile began a new era in exoplanet exploration. Though every planet in the TRAPPIST-1 system has been exciting, TRAPPIST-1e may be one of the best candidates for Earth-like conditions so far. It orbits in the Habitable Zone, is similar to Earth's mass, radius, and density, and recieves a similar amount of energy from its star. The atmospheres of the TRAPPIST-1 system require more investigation. Current models show that TRAPPIST-1e could be a bare rock or may have a thick notrogen atmosphere, but its star is also likely stripping its atmosphere away.
